issues.issue: The $1,400 monthly protocol fee has no stated duration or end date, so how long it runs must be inferred from elsewhere. That is a latent gap but the amount and payment mechanism themselves are definite.

The same $1,400 monthly charge appears in Section 5 (Fees) of the License Agreement and again as 'PROTOCOLS $16,800.00' in the lease Rent clause, raising whether one or two obligations were created. The figures reconcile at twelve months, so the tension is thin.

The Lessee is identified only as 'the Clinic Operator' with the identifying blank unfilled, leaving open whether the individual signer or a clinic entity is bound. That identity question is exactly the sort a court is asked to resolve.

The term is said to begin 'the first day of the month following the date of shipment or delivery' for 'the period of months indicated in Block A,' but Block A states a 'Lease/License Start Date' instead of a number of months, and 'ONE YEAR' is appended by hand. Which start date and which duration governs is genuinely uncertain.

The lease term ('ONE YEAR') cannot be squared with Section 6.1 of the License Agreement, whose effective and expiry dates are left blank and which runs until terminated by Licensor. The two halves of the same instrument therefore have different durations.

Rent is 'the sum shown in Block B above,' but Block B's Rental and Total lines are blank, while the clause then recites 'EQUIPMENT $68,250.00 PROTOCOLS $16,800.00' without saying whether those are monthly or aggregate figures. The amount and timing of each payment are not ascertainable from the words.

The $16,800 'PROTOCOLS' figure duplicates the $1,400 monthly license fee imposed by Section 5 of the License Agreement, so it is unclear whether protocol charges are rent under the lease or fees under the license. That matters for the lease remedies and the Guaranty, which speaks only of the Lease Agreement.

The clause makes the lease term begin per Paragraph 1 absent objection notice, while Paragraph 1 keys the term to shipment or delivery and Block A recites a separate start date. The overlap is minor but leaves the commencement trigger doubled.

'Lessor shall repair defects to the equipment free of charge' sits directly against Paragraph 8 (Loss and Damage; Maintenance), which says Lessee shall keep the A.R.P. Trainers in good repair 'and any repair shall be at the Lessee's cost.' Who bears repair cost is genuinely contradictory.

The blanket disclaimer is qualified only by 'EXCEPT AS IS SPECIFICALLY PROVIDED HEREIN,' which must be read against the express repair Warranty paragraph immediately preceding it. The carve-out is workable but its reach over that warranty could be argued.

The cap on Lessor liability at rent paid coexists with Section 10.2 of the License Agreement's absolute bar on consequential damages and with the Warranty repair promise, but the two limitation regimes are not obviously irreconcilable. A court asked which limit applies to protocol fees would have some work to do.

The clause excepts obligations 'as provided in this Paragraph 13,' but this is not Paragraph 13 (Paragraph 13 is Assignment), so the exception points at nothing. That miswritten cross-reference changes what the sentence carves out.

Placing all repair cost on Lessee contradicts the Warranty paragraph, under which Lessor repairs defects 'free of charge' during the term absent Lessee misuse. The two allocations of repair cost cannot both operate.

The cover page states 'Filing Fees Lessor to pay' and 'Sales or Other Tax Included,' whereas this paragraph loads all fees, assessments and taxes on Lessee. The face sheet and the operative text allocate charges differently.

The default trigger for false representations refers to documents 'furnished to the Lessee in connection with the transaction,' plainly reversing the parties, since it is Lessee's representations to Lessor that are meant. The error changes whose misstatement causes default.

The indemnity is given by 'the Lessee' but the operative duties in the second half are imposed on 'the Licensee,' a term defined only in the separate License Agreement, and 'acting outside the scope of use' is nowhere defined. Whose obligation this is, and what falls outside the scope of use, is uncertain.

Interest runs 'at the highest rate permitted by the laws of the state whose laws govern this Agreement, but not to exceed 8% per annum,' which sets a formula whose two limbs may point to different numbers. The reference is workable but the internal cap makes the operative rate arguable.

This integration clause says the Lease alone 'constitutes the entire agreement between the parties,' yet Section 8 of the License Agreement says the same of the License, and the lease Default paragraph expressly relies on breaches of the License and other contemporaneous agreements. The two integration clauses cannot both be literally true.

Venue is 'limited to the Hennepin County, Minnesota, Federal or State District Court to the exclusion of all other courts,' but there is no federal district court of Hennepin County, so whether the clause designates the District of Minnesota or only the state court is genuinely contestable. Its mandatory scope, 'enforcement of this Agreement,' also invites argument about which claims it captures.

The identical venue provision appears in Section 7(2) of the License Agreement, so a dispute spanning both instruments must be allocated between two separately worded but overlapping clauses. Their coexistence is more duplicative than contradictory.

The lease permits notice by personal delivery, telegram or first class mail, while Section 9 of the License Agreement requires facsimile or overnight courier. A notice good under one half of the instrument may be bad under the other.

The direction that an over-broad provision 'shall be sufficiently narrowed so as to make it enforceable' gives no standard for how far to narrow, which matters most for the two-year non-compete. What a narrowed clause would say is left entirely open.

The Licensee is left blank in the naming clause, and Section 1.4 ('Licensee shall refer to ___') is blank as well, so the identity of the contracting party is not stated. Whether the individual signer or a clinic entity is the Licensee is a live construction question.

The recital defines 'System(s)' to include Ultra Fit Athletic Mastery Protocols, but the operative grant in Section 2.1 licenses 'Accelerated Recovery Performance Protocols, In Balance Muscle Testing Protocols, Wave Site Protocols' instead. Recital and grant do not describe the same subject matter.

The recital subjects the license to Licensor's 'ongoing monitoring, revision, upgrading... in its sole and absolute discretion,' a power the operative text confers only partly (Section 2.4 enhancements) and never as a monitoring right. Recital and operative terms describe different bargains.

'System(s)' is defined by an open-ended tail — 'related programs, and related intellectual property' and 'all other intellectual property associated with' the named protocols — so the boundary of the defined term cannot be fixed. Whether a given protocol or program falls inside it drives the non-compete and confidentiality obligations.

The defined Systems list (Accelerated Recovery Program, Ultra Fit Athletic Mastery, In Balance Muscle Testing) does not match the Systems actually licensed in Section 2.1, which names Accelerated Recovery Performance and Wave Site Protocols. The definition and the grant are out of alignment.

'Licensee is granted no right, title or license to, or interest in, any ARP Trademarks' sits against Section 2.2, which gives Licensee the right to operate its clinic under the business name 'ARP Wave Clinic.' Whether the trade name may be used, and on what footing, is left inconsistent.

The grant licenses 'Accelerated Recovery Performance Protocols' and 'Wave Site Protocols,' neither of which appears in the Section 1.1 definition of System(s), and omits the Ultra Fit protocols that definition includes. What was actually licensed cannot be settled without choosing between the two lists.

The name right lasts 'for as long as the Licensee fully complies and is not in breach of this or any other agreements with ARP Wave, LLC,' with no materiality threshold and an unbounded reference to 'any other agreements.' What breach forfeits the right is left at large.

This right to trade as an 'ARP Wave Clinic' is difficult to square with Section 1.3, which grants Licensee 'no right, title or license to, or interest in, any ARP Trademarks.' One clause confers a naming right the other withholds.

Rights are said to be 'forfeitable in the event of certain circumstances or occurrences as herein set forth' without identifying which circumstances, leaving the forfeiture trigger to be assembled from elsewhere. The phrase 'certain circumstances or occurrences' has no ascertainable content on its face.

On assignment the clause says 'this Licensor shall then have no responsibility or liability... whatsoever to Licensee,' a garbled sentence ('this Licensor') whose subject and effect are unclear. Whether the assignor or the assignee is released turns on that slip.

The support promised — 'Monthly seminars in Minneapolis, Minnesota, Telephone Consultation and Email Support' — is stated without any measure of frequency, scope or responsiveness for the consultation and email limbs. What performance discharges the obligation is not fixed.

The requirement of 'trained medical personnel on site daily in the form of either a DC, DO, MD, PT' is a closed list whose exclusion of other credentialed staff is uncertain, and the exclusivity ban on 'any other type of physical therapy, training or rehabilitative service' is drafted without limit. Whether a clinic's ordinary practice breaches it is contestable.

'Perform in a professional manner,' 'any reasonable guidelines issued by ARP Wave' and conduct that 'reflects favorably' are standards with no benchmark stated in the Agreement. Whether conduct breaches them cannot be resolved from the words.

The restraint is bounded by 'the Territory defined in the Exclusive Licensee Agreement executed by the parties,' but no Exclusive Licensee Agreement forms part of this instrument and no Territory is defined anywhere in it. The geographic scope of the covenant therefore cannot be determined from the contract as a whole.

The prohibited activity — representing 'any similar or competitive system or Licensee' — is both garbled ('or Licensee') and unbounded ('similar'), so the conduct restrained is not identifiable. A two-year post-termination restraint of that width invites construction against the drafter.

The $1,400 monthly license fee duplicates the 'ADDITIONAL PROVISIONS' charge on the cover page and the 'PROTOCOLS $16,800.00' line in the lease Rent clause, and its duration depends on the blank term in Section 6.1. Whether one obligation or several were created is not clear from the instrument.

Both the effective date and the expiry date are left blank, and the sentence reads 'shall be continue in full force and effect until unless otherwise terminated,' which is ungrammatical and leaves no ascertainable term. The duration of the license cannot be read off the clause.

Only Licensor is given a right to terminate here, which cannot be squared with Section 6.3's automatic termination events or with the one-year term stated in Paragraph 1 of the Equipment Lease. How long the license runs depends on which of these controls.

Providing that all 'covenants and provisions herein set forth shall survive such termination, except those covenants as pertaining to future payments' makes the whole agreement perpetual in substance, and the exception's boundary ('future payments') is undefined. Which obligations genuinely survive is open.

Blanket survival is hard to reconcile with Section 2.2, under which the right to operate lasts only 'during the term,' and with Section 11.2, which requires immediate return of all Systems on termination. Read literally, terminated obligations both end and continue.

'Or other adverse creditor action' is a catch-all appended to the enumerated judgment, levy, lien, attachment and foreclosure notice, and its reach beyond those specifics is uncertain. Automatic forfeiture turns on where that general phrase stops.

Default may be declared 'if Licensor deems itself insecure,' a wholly subjective trigger with no reasonableness standard, and default under 'any other agreement entered into between Licensor and Licensee' is unbounded. Whether a purported default is valid is left to be construed.

Venue is confined to 'the Hennepin County, Minnesota, Federal or State District Court,' but no federal district court sits for Hennepin County, so whether the District of Minnesota is a permitted forum is genuinely arguable. The scope phrase 'enforcement of this Agreement' also leaves tort and related claims uncertain.

The clause duplicates Section 21 of the Equipment Lease in slightly different words, so a single dispute arising under both halves of the instrument is governed by two overlapping venue provisions. The duplication is awkward rather than contradictory.

The License Agreement declares itself the entire agreement 'regarding the subject matter hereof,' while Paragraph 18 of the Equipment Lease says the Lease is the entire agreement between the same parties, and both are executed as one document. Which integration clause bounds the bargain is unresolved.

Requiring notices by facsimile or overnight courier conflicts with Paragraph 22 of the Equipment Lease, which allows personal delivery, telegram or first class mail. A notice of default touching both agreements could satisfy one clause and fail the other.

The carve-out for 'THE EXPRESS WARRANTIES, IF ANY, MADE IN THE ARP WAVE LEASE AND LICENSE AGREEMENT' must be read against the Lease's Warranty paragraph promising free repair of defects. Whether that repair promise survives this disclaimer is arguable.

The first sentence preserves claims for 'breach or breaches of Licensor's contractual obligations,' while the second waives all rights to claim 'fraud, inaccuracy, imperfection of the System(s)' — an exception and a waiver that overlap. How far the preserved contract claim survives the fraud waiver is unclear.

The disclaimer of any representation as to 'effectiveness... or usefulness of the System(s)' pulls against the recital that Licensor owns and licenses proprietary rehabilitative protocols and against Section 3's promised support. The tension is real but not plainly irreconcilable.

'Any rights herein set forth shall be deemed to be automatically revoked and automatically reassigned to Licensor' does not distinguish Licensee's rights from Licensor's, and rights never assigned to Licensee cannot be 'reassigned.' The class of rights reverting is not identified.

Automatic revocation of 'any rights herein set forth' on termination is hard to square with Section 6.2, under which all covenants and provisions survive termination. One clause extinguishes what the other preserves.

The Agreement contains no clause headed confidentiality or non-disclosure beyond the proprietary-rights language of Section 4.5, so which provisions this survival clause preserves is uncertain. The clause points at a category the instrument never labels.

Disclaiming any 'franchise' relationship sits uneasily with the operative scheme of trade-name use, mandated training, exclusivity and monthly fees created by Sections 2.2, 4.1 and 5. Whether the disclaimer controls the substance is a question a court could be asked.

The Guaranty covers 'all indebtedness and liability which Lessee/Licensee may have to Lessor/Licensor under this Lease Agreement,' though the instrument comprises both a Lease and a separate License Agreement with its own $1,400 monthly fees. Whether the license obligations are guaranteed turns on that single reference.
The guarantor is identified only as 'the undersigned' with the Guarantor signature line blank, so who is personally bound is not stated. That identity gap is the sort of thing litigated directly.
